requirements: The core microarchitectural findings of the paper 'Dissecting the NVIDIA Volta GPU Architecture via Microbenchmarking' have been reproduced through microbenchmarks on a Volta V100 GPU.

sub_tasks.requirements: A Volta V100 GPU (PCIe form factor, and optionally SXM2/NVLink) with the CUDA 9.0 toolkit, nvcc, nvdisasm, cuobjdump, and cuBLAS is available; graphics clock is pinned to the reference values (1,380 MHz for V100 PCIe, 1,530 MHz for V100 NVLink, 1,328 MHz for P100 PCIe) so that clock-cycle measurements are reproducible.

GPU hardware is detected and reported as an NVIDIA Volta V100 (compute capability 7.0, GV100 chip) with an accompanying environment probe that stores the detected device name, PCI bus id, and compute capability to a machine-readable artifact used by later benchmarks.

Code has been implemented that queries the primary CUDA device (via cudaGetDeviceProperties or `nvidia-smi --query-gpu=name,pci.bus_id,compute_cap`) and writes the results (device name, PCI bus id, major/minor compute capability) to a JSON or text file in the results directory.

The environment probe fails loudly (non-zero exit code and a descriptive stderr message) when the detected device is not a Volta V100 (i.e. compute capability != 7.0 or device-name string does not contain 'V100'), so that microbenchmarks meant for GV100 are never silently run on the wrong architecture.

The probe distinguishes the PCIe form factor from the SXM2/NVLink form factor of the V100 (e.g. by parsing `nvidia-smi -q` link/product-name output or by counting available NVLink peers), and records the detected form factor so the pipeline can enable or skip the Chapter 5 NVLink benchmarks accordingly.

The CUDA 9.0 toolkit and all developer utilities used by the paper (nvcc, nvdisasm, cuobjdump, cuBLAS) are installed and their versions are recorded, so that SASS disassembly, instruction encoding analysis, and cuBLAS matrix-multiplication benchmarks match the paper's toolchain.

Code has been implemented (e.g. a `setup_env.sh` or CI check) that verifies `nvcc --version` reports CUDA release 9.0 and aborts with a clear message if any other major/minor toolkit version is on PATH.

The environment setup verifies that `nvdisasm` and `cuobjdump` (from the CUDA 9.0 binary utilities package) are available on PATH and executable; both binaries are used to disassemble compiled cubins into 128-bit Volta instruction words with their control information.

The CUDA 9.0 cuBLAS library (libcublas.so.9.0) is discoverable at link and runtime for the floating-point matrix-multiplication benchmarks; a smoke test loads the library and prints its reported version to confirm the correct SO is picked up rather than a newer system-installed cuBLAS.

All CUDA sources for the microbenchmarks are compiled with `nvcc -arch=sm_70` (Volta) using CUDA 9.0 so that the emitted SASS uses the Volta 128-bit instruction encoding studied in Chapter 2 rather than sm_60/sm_61 code.

The GPU graphics clocks are pinned to the paper's reference values before every timing benchmark, and the achieved clock is verified so that cycle-count and GB/s measurements are reproducible against the paper.

Code has been implemented (e.g. `pin_clocks.sh`) that invokes `nvidia-smi -pm 1` (persistence mode) and `nvidia-smi -ac <memclock>,<gfxclock>` (or `-lgc` for a locked graphics clock) with elevated privileges, and returns a non-zero exit code if pinning fails.
On a V100 PCIe board, the graphics clock is pinned to 1,380 MHz (the peak graphics clock reported in Table 3.1 and used for cuBLAS TFLOPS reporting in Section 4.4).
On a V100 SXM2/NVLink board, the graphics clock is pinned to 1,530 MHz as used in Chapter 5's NVLink benchmarks.

When a Pascal P100 PCIe reference board is available for cross-architecture comparisons, its graphics clock is pinned to 1,328 MHz (Table 3.1) prior to running the shared latency/bandwidth benchmarks.

After pinning, code samples the current SM clock (via `nvidia-smi --query-gpu=clocks.sm --format=csv,noheader,nounits` or NVML) and asserts that the observed frequency is within +/-1% of the requested reference value; the assertion runs before each benchmark suite to catch thermal throttling or unpinning between runs.

The environment state that could distort microbenchmark numbers (ECC on/off, driver version, shared-memory carveout) is captured for the record so that reported numbers can be interpreted alongside the paper's setup.

Code has been implemented that queries and records the NVIDIA driver version, ECC state (`nvidia-smi -q -d ECC`), and installed CUDA runtime/driver API versions to the results directory before benchmarks run.

For L1-data-cache / shared-memory benchmarks the shared-memory carveout is configured explicitly (via `cudaFuncSetAttribute` with `cudaFuncAttributePreferredSharedMemoryCarveout` or `cudaDeviceSetSharedMemConfig`) to the {0, 64, 96} KiB shared-memory sizes used in Table 3.3 so the effective L1 data cache size is deterministic across runs.

The motivational 8x8 register-tile FFMA inner kernel is compiled with NVCC 9.0, binary-patched to remove register-bank conflicts and leverage the register reuse cache as in Table 1.1, and the reported per-SMX GFlops/s improvement is reproduced.
The CUDA source for the motivational 8x8 register-tile GEMM inner kernel from Chapter 1 is implemented.
Code has been implemented that declares __shared__ float shr_A[8*512] and shr_B[8*512] and register-mapped arrays float reg_A[8], reg_B[8], reg_C[64] matching the Chapter 1 listing.
Code has been implemented that iterates the k-loop from 0 to 512 and, per iteration, loads reg_A[i]=shr_A[i+k*8] and reg_B[i]=shr_B[i+k*8] for i in [0,8).

Code has been implemented for the 8x8 outer-product accumulation reg_C[i*8+j] += reg_A[i]*reg_B[j] for i,j in [0,8), yielding an inner loop that generates 64 FFMA per k-iteration as expected by Table 1.1.
NVCC 9.0 compilation of the motivational kernel for sm_70 and SASS extraction infrastructure exist.
Code has been implemented that invokes NVCC from the CUDA 9.0 toolkit with -arch=sm_70 to produce a cubin/executable for the motivational kernel and fails loudly if a non-9.0 nvcc is used.

Code has been implemented that runs nvdisasm/cuobjdump on the compiled cubin to extract the SASS listing for the inner kernel and locates the contiguous block of FFMA instructions constituting the 8x8 tile update.
Code has been implemented that parses each FFMA line into (dst, srcA, srcB, srcC) register operands together with any .reuse annotations, using a regex/tokenizer that matches nvdisasm output.

The extracted baseline FFMA sequence reproduces the left column of Table 1.1: 64 FFMA instructions with the exact destination and source register indices listed (e.g. FFMA R16, R12, R80, R16; FFMA R17, R80.reuse, R13, R17; ...; FFMA R79, R11, R7, R79).
Register bank conflict analysis for Volta's 2-bank, 64-bit-wide register file is implemented.
Code has been implemented for a bank-assignment function bank(reg_idx) = reg_idx % 2 that classifies each general-purpose register into bank 0 or bank 1.
Code has been implemented that flags an FFMA as bank-conflicted when its three 32-bit source registers all lie in the same bank and no .reuse of the offending operand is present on the instruction.

The analyzer flags FFMA R16, R12, R80, R16 as a bank-0 conflict and FFMA R25, R13, R81, R25 / FFMA R31, R11, R81, R31 / FFMA R43, R15, R83, R43 as bank-1 conflicts, matching the four instructions singled out in Chapter 1.
Code has been implemented that reports the total number of bank-conflicted FFMA in the NVCC 9.0 baseline sequence and confirms it is strictly greater than zero.
Register-reuse-cache modeling for the four operand slots is implemented.

Code has been implemented that models the 4 register reuse caches (one per source operand slot) so that a source marked .reuse in instruction N is available to instruction N+1 in the same slot without a bank read.
Code has been implemented that treats a source register whose value is already in its slot's reuse cache as consuming no bank read for that instruction when evaluating conflicts.
Binary patching pipeline that rewrites the SASS to the improved mapping of Table 1.1 (right column) is implemented.
Code has been implemented that rewrites the cubin at the binary level (patching FFMA operand encodings and reuse flags in place) rather than re-emitting via nvcc.

The patched SASS matches the right column of Table 1.1 instruction-for-instruction (e.g. FFMA R17, R12.reuse, R80.reuse, R17 as the first FFMA and FFMA R22, R12.reuse, R7, R22 as the last), preserving destination assignments consistent with Figure 1.1's improved register mapping.
Re-running the bank-conflict analyzer on the patched SASS reports zero remaining FFMA bank conflicts after accounting for .reuse flags.

Code has been implemented that validates numerical equivalence between the baseline kernel and the patched kernel by comparing the resulting reg_C tile (or its stored output) bit-for-bit on a fixed input, ensuring the patch did not change semantics.
Benchmark harness that measures per-SMX GFlops/s of the inner kernel with 128 threads is implemented.
Code has been implemented that launches the kernel with 128 threads per block (4 warps, matching the paper's stated minimum for full processing-unit utilization) on a single SM.
Code has been implemented that times the kernel using CUDA events (or %clock reads) and computes GFlops/s from the total FMA count (2 flops per FFMA * 64 FFMA/iter * 512 iterations * 128 threads).

Code has been implemented that normalizes throughput to per-SMX GFlops/s (i.e., divides by number of active SMs = 1 or by the total SM count when running many blocks) matching Chapter 1's reporting convention.

Code has been implemented that pins the V100 graphics clock (e.g. via nvidia-smi -lgc) to the 1,380 MHz PCIe peak used elsewhere in the paper so throughput numbers are comparable, and records the clock actually observed.
The per-SMX GFlops/s numbers reported in Chapter 1 for the baseline and patched kernel are reproduced.
The unmodified, NVCC 9.0-compiled inner kernel measured with 128 threads achieves 132.05 GFlops/s per SMX on V100.
The binary-patched inner kernel (conflict-free mapping + reuse-cache exploitation) measured with 128 threads achieves 152.43 GFlops/s per SMX on V100.
The relative speedup of the patched kernel over the NVCC 9.0 baseline is +15.4% (i.e., 152.43/132.05 - 1), reproducing the improvement quoted in Chapter 1.

The Volta 128-bit instruction word layout (91-bit instruction, 23-bit control, 14 unused bits), the 6-field control section (reuse flags, wait barrier mask, read/write barrier index, yield flag, stall cycles), and the opcode placement in the low bits of the first 64-bit half (10-13 bit opcodes) have been characterized via exhaustive disassembly.
A disassembly harness that exhaustively enumerates SASS instructions and extracts raw 128-bit words is in place, forming the basis for encoding claims.

Code has been implemented that invokes nvdisasm (from the CUDA 9.0 toolkit) on compiled Volta (sm_70) cubins and captures both the disassembled mnemonic and the two 64-bit hex words per instruction line.

Code has been implemented that generates a broad corpus of Volta SASS instructions (covering FFMA, IADD3, LOP3, HMMA, memory loads/stores, control-flow, etc.) so that opcode and control-field distributions can be sampled across the ISA rather than a single instruction.

A bit-field extractor is implemented that takes the two 64-bit words per Volta instruction, concatenates them into a 128-bit integer, and provides deterministic accessors for arbitrary bit-ranges (used by every downstream field-layout leaf).
The high-level 128-bit Volta word layout (91 instruction bits, 23 control bits, 14 unused bits) is measured from exhaustive disassembly and matches the paper.

Code has been implemented that verifies each Volta instruction occupies exactly one 128-bit word rendered by nvdisasm as two contiguous 64-bit hex halves, and that the first half is 'instruction only' while the second half carries both instruction bits and control bits (matching the paper's illustrated split).

Across the exhaustive disassembly corpus, at least 91 of the 128 bits per word are measured to encode instruction (opcode + operands) information, reproducing the paper's '≥91 instruction bits' claim.

Across the disassembly corpus, at least 23 bits per 128-bit word are measured to encode control information (the 21-bit control section plus its 2 zero MSBs), reproducing the paper's '≥23 control bits' claim.
The remaining 14 bits per Volta 128-bit word are measured to appear unused (constant or invariant) across the exhaustive disassembly, reproducing the paper's '14 unused bits' claim.

Code has been implemented that demonstrates the control section is preceded and followed by instruction encoding bits within the 128-bit word (i.e., control bits are embedded, not appended), rather than being bundled separately as on Pascal/Maxwell.

The 21-bit Volta control section is decomposed into its six named fields with the exact bit widths reported in the paper (reuse:4, wait mask:6, read idx:3, write idx:3, yield:1, stall:4) plus 2 leading zero bits.
Code has been implemented that isolates the 21-bit control section per Volta instruction and verifies its 2 most-significant bits are always zero across the disassembly corpus.

Code has been implemented that extracts a 4-bit 'reuse flags' field from each control section, with the field position such that the LSB of the nibble controls the first source-operand slot and the MSB controls the fourth source-operand slot (matching the paper's Section 2.1).

Code has been implemented that extracts a 6-bit 'wait barrier mask' field and treats it as a bitmask over the 6 available barriers (not an index), consistent with the paper's statement that an instruction may wait on multiple barriers.

Code has been implemented that extracts a 3-bit 'read barrier index' field, and validates that observed values lie in 0..7 (indexing at most 6 barriers plus a 'none' state) across the disassembly corpus.

Code has been implemented that extracts a 3-bit 'write barrier index' field and validates it is populated on variable-latency writes (e.g., memory loads) and left at the 'none' encoding on typical fixed-latency ALU ops.
Code has been implemented that extracts a 1-bit 'yield flag' field from the control section for every instruction in the corpus.
Code has been implemented that extracts a 4-bit 'stall cycles' field and verifies observed values span the full 0..15 range (matching the paper's stated 0-15 cycle window).

Code has been implemented that reassembles the six fields (4+6+3+3+1+4 = 21 bits) plus the 2 zero MSBs and reproduces the original 23-bit control payload bit-for-bit, providing a round-trip check on the layout.
The behavioral semantics of the yield flag and stall cycles fields are validated on Volta (single dispatcher per processing block, no observable dual-issue; one-cycle warp-switch cost).

Code has been implemented that scans compiled Volta code for the special (stall,yield) bit combination that triggers dual-issue on Pascal/Maxwell, and confirms it never occurs (or never produces two-issue behavior) in NVCC-generated Volta code.

A microbenchmark demonstrates that flipping the yield flag on a run of independent instructions costs one extra cycle per warp switch, consistent with the paper's description of the yield flag's cost.
The Volta opcode placement (least-significant bits of the first 64-bit half) and opcode length range (10-13 bits) are characterized via exhaustive disassembly and match the paper.

Code has been implemented that, for each disassembled Volta instruction, extracts a candidate opcode from the least-significant bits of the first 64-bit half of the 128-bit word and confirms this bit range partitions instructions consistently by mnemonic (i.e., all FFMA share one opcode value, all IADD3 share another, etc.).

The measured Volta opcode width, determined by finding the minimum number of low bits that uniquely separates all observed mnemonics, falls within the 10-13 bit range reported in the paper (Section 2.3).

Code has been implemented that produces an opcode reference table (mnemonic -> opcode bits, opcode width) for Volta covering at least the instructions listed in Table 4.1 of the paper (IADD3, SHF, LOP3, SEL, MOV, FADD, FFMA, FMUL, IMAD, DADD, DMUL, DFMA, HADD2, HMUL2, HFMA2, POPC, FLO, MUFU, HMMA, etc.).

A comparison check shows that on Volta the opcode is in the LOW bits of the first 64-bit half, whereas on a Pascal (sm_60/sm_61) reference disassembly the opcode lies in the HIGH bits of the 64-bit instruction word, reproducing the paper's departure claim.
Operand encoding on Volta (register / memory / immediate) and predication encoding (4 bits: 1 negation + 3 predicate register index) are characterized.

Code has been implemented that identifies a 4-bit predication field per Volta instruction consisting of a 1-bit negation flag and a 3-bit predicate register index, and verifies this by comparing '@P0'/'@!P0'/... prefixes emitted by nvdisasm against the extracted bit pattern across the corpus.

Code has been implemented that classifies each disassembled Volta operand into one of {general-purpose register, special register, predicate register, constant memory address, shared memory address, global memory address, immediate}, matching the operand taxonomy in Section 2.3.

Code has been implemented that produces a cross-architecture comparison of instruction/control encoding, contrasting Volta's single 128-bit-per-instruction embedded layout against Pascal/Maxwell's bundle of 1 control word + 3 instruction words and Kepler's 1+7 bundle, matching Section 2.1 of the paper.

The scheduler_id = warp_id % 4 mapping onto the four processing blocks of a Volta SM is demonstrated by an 8-warp benchmark in which two FFMA-issuing warps sweep all pairings from Table 2.1, and the per-configuration GFLOPS reproduce the ~42 vs ~66 GFLOPS collision/no-collision pattern reported in the paper.

The Section 2.2 benchmark kernel is implemented: it launches exactly 8 warps on a single Volta SM, keeps 6 warps idle while 2 designated warps (warp A and warp B) issue an FFMA sequence long enough to yield a stable throughput measurement in GFLOPS.

Code has been implemented that launches a single CUDA block containing exactly 8 warps (256 threads) on one Volta V100 SM (e.g. a single-block grid with 256 threads pinned to one SM), matching the 8-warp configuration described in Section 2.2.

Code has been implemented so that inside the kernel only the two warps whose indices equal the configured `warp_A_idx` and `warp_B_idx` execute the FFMA sequence, while the remaining 6 warps take an early-return / idle path and issue no FFMA work.

Code has been implemented such that the active warps execute a long, dependency-controlled sequence of FFMA (single-precision fused multiply-add) instructions (issued via inline PTX/SASS or an unrolled loop) with enough iterations that the measured throughput is dominated by steady-state FFMA issue rather than start-up overhead.

Code has been implemented that exposes `warp_A_idx` and `warp_B_idx` as configurable inputs (e.g. kernel arguments, template parameters, or launch parameters) so the same kernel can be driven through every (A, B) combination from Table 2.1 without recompiling per pair.

Code has been implemented that converts the measured runtime and number of FFMA operations issued by the two active warps into a single-precision arithmetic throughput expressed in GFLOPS (matching the units used in Table 2.1), using the V100's operating clock and 2 flops/FFMA.
The benchmark harness sweeps the full 4x4 grid of warp pairings from Table 2.1 and emits per-pair GFLOPS in a form directly comparable to the paper's table.

Code has been implemented that iterates over all 16 (warp_A_idx, warp_B_idx) combinations with warp_A_idx in {0, 1, 2, 3} and warp_B_idx in {4, 5, 6, 7}, invoking the benchmark kernel once per pair and recording the resulting GFLOPS.

Code has been implemented that writes the 16 measured GFLOPS values into a 4x4 result table (rows indexed by warp B in 4..7, columns indexed by warp A in 0..3) mirroring the layout of Table 2.1, and persists it to disk (e.g. CSV/JSON) for grading.

The measured 4x4 throughput table reproduces the collision-vs-no-collision pattern of Table 2.1: same-processing-block pairs (A % 4 == B % 4) collapse to roughly half the throughput of different-processing-block pairs, matching the ~42 GFLOPS vs ~66 GFLOPS values in the paper.

For every (warp_A_idx, warp_B_idx) pair where warp_A_idx % 4 == warp_B_idx % 4 (the four 'diagonal' entries of Table 2.1: (0,4), (1,5), (2,6), (3,7)), the measured single-precision throughput is close to ~42 GFLOPS (Table 2.1 values 42.27, 41.98, 42.06, 42.08).

For every (warp_A_idx, warp_B_idx) pair where warp_A_idx % 4 != warp_B_idx % 4 (the twelve off-diagonal entries of Table 2.1), the measured single-precision throughput is close to ~66 GFLOPS (Table 2.1 off-diagonal values cluster around 66.02-66.05).

The ratio between the mean off-diagonal throughput and the mean diagonal throughput is close to the ~1.57x factor implied by Table 2.1 (~66/~42), demonstrating that a single processing block halves throughput relative to two distinct blocks.
The benchmark output is analyzed to derive the two conclusions the paper draws from Table 2.1: the scheduler_id = warp_id % 4 mapping and the ≥128-threads-required rule.

Code has been implemented that programmatically classifies each (warp_A_idx, warp_B_idx) pair as 'same processing block' iff warp_A_idx % 4 == warp_B_idx % 4, then asserts/reports that this classification exactly matches the low-throughput cells of the measured 4x4 table, thereby verifying the `scheduler_id = warp_id % 4` mapping.

The analysis report explicitly states the Section 2.2 corollary that at least 128 threads (4 warps, one per processing block) are required to fully utilize a Volta SM's processing units, and justifies it from the measured throughput doubling when the two active warps land on different processing blocks.

Volta's combined L1 data cache is characterized on a V100: 28-cycle hit latency (vs. 84 on Pascal), 32-128 KiB configurable size, 32 B line, 128 B update granularity, 4 sets, non-LRU replacement, ~108.3 bytes/cycle/SM measured bandwidth (256 B/cycle theoretical upper bound), and the ~7 KiB shortfall observed by fine-grained pointer chase (detected 121/57/25 KiB when shared memory is configured to 0/64/96 KiB).
A fine-grained pointer-chase infrastructure (per Mei and Chu) is implemented that is reused by the L1 latency, geometry, and replacement-policy experiments.

Code has been implemented that allocates a global-memory linked list whose stride, array length, and element type are configurable so the same kernel can sweep sizes across the full 32-128 KiB configurable L1 range and beyond.

Code has been implemented for a CUDA pointer-chase kernel where each iteration issues a `ld.global.ca` load whose result address feeds the next load, forcing a data dependency and preventing the compiler/hardware from overlapping accesses.

The pointer-chase kernel performs a warm-up traversal that populates L1 before timing, and only records per-access clocks from a second traversal (so that steady-state L1-hit behavior — not cold-miss behavior — is reported).

Code has been implemented that reads the SM cycle counter via the `%clock` special register (or `CS2R`/`clock64`) around individual loads and produces a per-access latency array that downstream analysis converts into the Figure 3.2 latency curve.
The L1 data-cache hit latency on Volta V100 is measured, matched against Pascal for context, and the Figure 3.2 latency signature (28 / 193 / 375 / 1029 cycles) is reproduced.

Code has been implemented that classifies each pointer-chase access into L1 hit, L2 hit, or L2-miss+TLB-hit buckets by inspecting stride relative to the 32 B L1 line and 64 B L2 line, matching the analysis Mei-and-Chu use to build Figure 3.2.
The measured average L1-hit latency on V100 is ~28 clock cycles, matching Table 3.1 / Figure 3.2 for accesses served from the L1 data cache.

The reported Pascal comparison L1-hit latency is ~84 cycles (either measured on a P100/P4 if available or quoted from the paper's Table 3.1 value of 82), so the Volta-vs-Pascal ~3x latency improvement is documented alongside the Volta measurement.
The Figure 3.2 first-access latency of ~1029 cycles (L2 miss + TLB miss) is reproduced from the pointer chase, distinguishing it from steady-state L1/L2 hit accesses.
The Figure 3.2 intermediate latency plateaus of ~193 cycles (L1 miss / L2 hit) and ~375 cycles (L2 miss / TLB hit) are reproduced from the same pointer-chase run.
The L1 data-cache load bandwidth benchmark of Listing 3.1 is implemented and used to reproduce the ~108.3 B/cycle/SM measured throughput against the 256 B/cycle theoretical upper bound.

Code has been implemented for a `l1_bw` CUDA kernel matching Listing 3.1: warm-up loop that populates the L1 with 64-bit doubles, followed by a timed loop where every warp scans every element in the cached region.

The bandwidth kernel issues loads via inline PTX `ld.global.ca.f64` (cache-all, 64-bit double) and accumulates each loaded value into a register-resident `sink` so the compiler cannot dead-code-eliminate the loads.

Warps are synchronized with `bar.sync 0` before and after the timed region, and the elapsed cycle count is captured via `mov.u32 %0, %%clock` before/after so that a per-SM cycle window can be extracted.
Code has been implemented that converts recorded (cycles, bytes-loaded) pairs into bytes-per-cycle-per-SM, dividing total bytes by the maximum cycle window across threads on a single SM.
The measured L1 load throughput on V100 is ~108.3 bytes/cycle/SM, reproducing the value tabulated in Table 3.2 for the Volta L1 bandwidth benchmark.

Code has been implemented that computes the 256 bytes/cycle/SM theoretical upper bound from LSU count per SM × bytes per LSU per cycle, and reports it alongside the measured V100 number as in Table 3.2.

The L1 data-cache geometry is characterized: configurable 32-128 KiB size, the ~7 KiB detection shortfall observed via fine-grained pointer chase (121 / 57 / 25 KiB detected for shared-memory carveouts of 0 / 64 / 96 KiB), plus the 32 B line size, 32 B load granularity, 128 B update granularity, and 4 sets.

Code has been implemented that configures the combined L1/shared subsystem to shared-memory carveouts of 0, 64, and 96 KiB (e.g., via `cudaFuncSetAttribute` with `cudaFuncAttributePreferredSharedMemoryCarveout`) so the corresponding L1 targets of 128, 64, and 32 KiB can be probed.

Code has been implemented that sweeps array size `A` in fine-grained steps and detects the L1 capacity as the largest working-set size for which the second pointer-chase pass shows no L1 misses, matching the Table 3.3 methodology.
The detected L1 data-cache size is ~121 KiB when the shared-memory carveout is 0 KiB (nominal 128 KiB L1), matching Table 3.3.
The detected L1 data-cache size is ~57 KiB when the shared-memory carveout is 64 KiB (nominal 64 KiB L1), matching Table 3.3.
The detected L1 data-cache size is ~25 KiB when the shared-memory carveout is 96 KiB (nominal 32 KiB L1), matching Table 3.3.

Across all three shared-memory configurations, the detected L1 size falls ~7 KiB short of the nominal L1 capacity, and this shortfall is explicitly reported and attributed to the replacement policy (rather than to ECC).
Code has been implemented that measures the L1 line size from the pointer-chase stride at which consecutive addresses stop sharing a hit — the reported Volta L1 line size is 32 B (Table 3.1).
Code has been implemented that measures the L1 load granularity by observing that a single miss brings in exactly 32 B, matching the 32 B load-granularity entry of Table 3.1.
Code has been implemented that measures the L1 update (fill) granularity — the paper reports 128 B for Volta — by showing that a single miss updates a 128 B aligned region rather than a 32 B line.

Code has been implemented that measures the L1 associativity/number of sets: the paper reports 4 sets on Volta (Table 3.1), and the benchmark reproduces this by identifying that only 4 lines conflict for a given index bit pattern.

Code has been implemented that confirms the Volta L1 data cache is virtually indexed (not physical) by reproducing the paper's TLB-vs-L1 experiment: an array that exceeds L1-TLB coverage but fits in L1 shows no TLB miss in the second scan when L1 is enabled.

The non-LRU L1 replacement policy is characterized — specifically that four cache lines from four different sets are the first to be evicted when L1 saturates, giving large arrays higher preservation priority than sparse accesses.

Code has been implemented for a benchmark that first fully populates L1, then issues a controlled additional load that must evict exactly one line, and records which of the previously cached lines becomes a miss on the next scan.
Code has been implemented that maps evicted lines back to their (set, way) coordinates so the eviction pattern can be characterized rather than reported only as an aggregate miss count.
The reproduced replacement-policy result shows exactly 4 cache lines — one from each of the 4 sets — are the first to be evicted, matching the paper's description of low-preservation-priority lines.

The reproduced policy is explicitly shown to be non-LRU: under an LRU control scenario the same evictions would not occur, and the run's report flags Volta's L1 update policy as `non-LRU` (matching the Table 3.1 entry, in contrast to Pascal's LRU).
The L1 data-cache findings are packaged into the paper's Table 3.1, Table 3.2, Table 3.3 rows and Figure 3.2 curve so downstream sections and reviewers can read the results directly.

Code has been implemented that emits the Table 3.1 L1-data row for V100 (size 32-128 KiB, line 32 B, hit latency 28, sets 4, load granularity 32 B, update granularity 128 B, update policy non-LRU, physical-indexed no) into the results directory.
Code has been implemented that emits the Table 3.2 L1 load throughput row for V100 (~108.3 B/cycle measured, 256 B/cycle theoretical) into the results directory.
Code has been implemented that emits the Table 3.3 detected-vs-expected L1 sizes ({0->128->121, 64->64->57, 96->32->25} KiB) into the results directory.
Code has been implemented that renders a Figure 3.2-style latency-vs-address plot with the 28 / 193 / 375 / 1029-cycle plateaus labelled, saved as a PNG/PDF under the results directory.
Volta's unified L2 is reproduced: 6,144 KiB capacity, 16-way associativity, 64 B line, ~193-cycle hit latency, physically indexed, and ~2,155 GB/s load throughput measured with Listing 3.2 on V100.
Benchmark infrastructure for probing the V100 L2 cache is implemented, including both the Listing 3.2 bandwidth kernel and the fine-grained p-chase machinery used for latency and geometry.

Code has been implemented reproducing the Listing 3.2 CUDA kernel `l2_bw` that iterates a `posArray` sized to the L2 capacity, has every warp load all elements, uses inline PTX `ld.global.cg.f64` followed by `add.f64` into a register accumulator, and writes the accumulator into `dsink` to prevent dead-code elimination.

Code has been implemented that warms the L2 cache (e.g., by an explicit warm-up kernel or preliminary scan) before the timed L2 bandwidth and latency kernels are launched, so measurements reflect L2 hits and not cold-miss / DRAM-fill behavior.

Code has been implemented reproducing Mei and Chu's fine-grained pointer-chase (p-chase) benchmark that traverses a global-memory linked-list-style buffer and records per-access latency using the `%%clock` special register, so that L2 hits are distinguishable from L1 hits, L2 misses, and TLB misses (as in Figure 3.2).

The benchmark driver launches kernels on the V100 with grid/block configurations chosen to saturate the L2 (e.g., enough threads and blocks so that LSU load-request throughput at the L2 is the bottleneck) and records elapsed clock cycles via `%%clock`/`%%clock64` or nvprof profiling counters, not via CPU-side wall time only.
L2 cache size is measured by sweeping the working set with a p-chase / bandwidth benchmark and detecting the transition from L2-hit latency to DRAM-hit latency.

Code has been implemented that sweeps the accessed array size across a range that brackets 6,144 KiB (e.g., from ~1 MiB to ~10 MiB) and, at each size, records the average per-access latency of a warm p-chase, producing a curve that plateaus at the L2-hit latency and steps up at the L2 capacity.

The L2-capacity detector identifies the smallest working-set size at which the average latency transitions from the L2-hit plateau to the DRAM-hit plateau, and emits it as the measured L2 size in KiB.
The measured L2 cache size on the V100 GPU is 6,144 KiB, matching Table 3.1's reported value.
L2 cache line size is determined by measuring which addresses share a fill on an L2 miss.

Code has been implemented that probes L2 line size by touching one address, then measuring latency for nearby addresses at increasing byte offsets to find the largest stride at which subsequent accesses still hit L2 without triggering another fill.
The measured L2 cache line size on the V100 GPU is 64 B, matching Table 3.1's reported value.
L2 cache associativity is inferred by measuring conflict misses across a set of addresses that map to the same L2 set.

Code has been implemented that constructs sequences of addresses spaced by `L2_size / num_sets` and increases the sequence length until conflict misses appear, thereby detecting L2 associativity via the number of ways that fit before eviction.
The measured L2 associativity on the V100 GPU is 16-way set-associative, matching the paper's statement in Section 3.2.
L2 hit latency on V100 is measured with the fine-grained p-chase experiment and shown to have the plateau shape of Figure 3.2.

Code has been implemented that, from the p-chase trace, extracts the four latency regimes visible in Figure 3.2 (L1 hit ~28 cycles, L1-miss/L2-hit ~193 cycles, L2-miss/TLB-hit ~375 cycles, cold miss with TLB miss ~1029 cycles) and reports them as classified plateaus.
The measured average L2 hit latency on the V100 GPU is approximately 193 clock cycles, matching Table 3.1 and Figure 3.2 within tolerance.

A plot reproducing Figure 3.2 (latency vs. relative memory address in bytes, with visible plateaus at ~28, ~193, ~375, and ~1029 cycles) is generated from the p-chase measurements and saved as an artifact of the L2 benchmark.
L2 cache is shown to be physically indexed by comparing TLB-miss behavior with L1 data cache enabled vs. disabled.

Code has been implemented that scans an array larger than the L1 TLB coverage in two configurations — L1 data cache enabled (via `ld.global.ca`) and L1 data cache disabled (via `ld.global.cg`) — and records TLB-miss latency signatures in each case, following Section 3.8's method.

When the L1 data cache is enabled, the second scan shows no TLB misses; when the L1 data cache is disabled (so accesses go to L2), TLB misses are observed — demonstrating that the L2 cache is indexed by physical addresses (Table 3.1: 'Physical address indexed: yes').
L2 load throughput is measured with the Listing 3.2 kernel and reported in GB/s for the V100 GPU (Table 3.4).

Code has been implemented that computes the L2 load throughput in GB/s from the Listing 3.2 kernel by dividing (total bytes loaded across all warps) by (measured elapsed clock cycles) and multiplying by the graphics clock frequency (1,380 MHz for V100).

The bandwidth kernel is invoked with an array sized to fit within the 6,144 KiB L2 (i.e., L2_SIZE constant), and every warp loads all in-L2 elements (double-nested loop pattern in Listing 3.2) to keep the L2 saturated for the duration of the timed region.
The measured L2 load throughput on the V100 GPU is approximately 2,155 GB/s, matching Table 3.4 within tolerance.
Results across the L2 experiments are consolidated into a report that matches the L2 row of Table 3.1 and the V100 column of Table 3.4.

A results artifact (e.g., `results/l2_cache.json` or a Markdown table) is emitted containing the fields Size (KiB), Line size (B), Associativity (ways), Hit latency (cycles), Physical-address-indexed (bool), Load throughput (GB/s), populated with the V100 measurements.

The results artifact's V100 entries reproduce the paper's Table 3.1 L2 row (6,144 KiB, 64 B line, ~193-cycle hit latency, physically indexed = yes) and Table 3.4 V100 throughput (~2,155 GB/s) within stated tolerances.

sub_tasks.requirements: The three-level Volta instruction cache is measured via FFMA-sequence inverse throughput plateaus: ~12 KiB L0 (private to a processing block, 3-way, 16 sets, 256 B line), 128 KiB L1 (private to an SM, 8-way, 32 sets, 512 B line), and the shared L2; the private/shared scopes are verified by the two-warp and two-SM thrashing experiments.
The core microbenchmark harness that emits long sequences of independent FFMA instructions, warms the instruction cache with a first pass, and times a second pass with the on-chip %clock register.

Code has been implemented that generates CUDA/PTX/SASS kernels containing configurable-length sequences of FFMA (single-precision fused multiply-add) instructions operating only on registers so that the data memory hierarchy is not exercised.

Code has been implemented that assigns FFMA operand registers so that no instruction has a read-after-write dependence on any of its neighbors in the sequence (enforced by verifying the assembled SASS destination/source register sets).

Code has been implemented that executes each FFMA sequence twice within a single kernel launch, records the clock only around the second execution, and returns cycles/instruction so that the instruction cache is warm when timing starts.

Code has been implemented that reads the per-SM %clock (or clock64) special register via inline PTX before and after the measured region and converts the difference into an inverse-throughput value normalized by the FFMA count.

Code has been implemented that pins the measurement to a single warp on a chosen processing block (via warp index modulo 4) and disables other warps so that the reported cycles/instruction reflect a single scheduler's issue rate.
The coarse FFMA-sequence-length sweep that reveals three plateaus corresponding to L0, L1 and L2 instruction cache hits (Figure 3.3, top and bottom rows for V100).
Code has been implemented that sweeps FFMA sequence sizes from below 4 KiB to at least 44 KiB on V100 in fine enough steps to render the three-plateau curve in the top-left panel of Figure 3.3.

Code has been implemented that extends the same sweep into the MiB range (roughly 5.6 to 6.8 MiB) so that the L2-to-global instruction fetch transition is visible in the bottom-left panel of Figure 3.3.

Code has been implemented that programmatically detects plateau boundaries in the inverse-throughput curve (change-point detection or fixed thresholds on cycles/instruction) and emits the (size, level) list.
The L0 plateau end measured on V100 corresponds to an L0 instruction cache size of approximately 12 KiB (matching the L0 row of Table 3.1 for GV100 and the L0 label in Figure 3.3).
The L1 plateau end measured on V100 corresponds to an L1 instruction cache size of 128 KiB (matching the L1 instruction row of Table 3.1 for GV100 and the L1 label in Figure 3.3).
The L2 instruction-cache plateau on V100 ends near a sequence size of approximately 6,144 KiB, consistent with the unified 6,144 KiB L2 reported in Table 3.1 (row L2 instruction).
The high-resolution FFMA sweep near the L0 boundary (Figure 3.4, left) that resolves L0 as a 3-way associative cache with 16 sets and a 256 B line.
Code has been implemented that sweeps FFMA sequence sizes with sub-256 B resolution across roughly 11-17 KiB and records inverse throughput per size (input to the left panel of Figure 3.4).

The high-resolution L0 sweep reveals exactly 16 discrete latency-step transitions between the L0-hit and L1-hit regimes (one transition per set), matching the 16-set L0 geometry claimed in Section 3.3.
The measured L0 associativity on V100 is 3-way (the number of stride-256 B addresses that co-reside in one L0 set before eviction), matching Section 3.3's claim.
The measured L0 line size on V100 is 256 B (derived from the granularity of the latency steps in the L0-boundary sweep), matching Section 3.3's claim.
The product of measured L0 sets (16) × associativity (3) × line size (256 B) equals approximately 12 KiB, consistent with the L0 instruction cache size reported in Table 3.1 for GV100.
The high-resolution FFMA sweep near the L1 boundary (Figure 3.4, right) that resolves L1 as an 8-way associative cache with 32 sets and a 512 B line.
Code has been implemented that sweeps FFMA sequence sizes with sub-512 B resolution across roughly 128-144 KiB and records inverse throughput per size (input to the right panel of Figure 3.4).
The high-resolution L1 sweep on V100 reveals exactly 32 discrete latency-step transitions between the L1-hit and L2-hit regimes, matching the 32-set L1 geometry claimed in Section 3.3.
The measured L1 associativity on V100 is 8-way (the number of stride-512 B addresses that co-reside in one L1 set before eviction), matching Section 3.3's claim.
The measured L1 line size on V100 is 512 B (derived from the granularity of the latency steps in the L1-boundary sweep), matching Section 3.3's claim.
The product of measured L1 sets (32) × associativity (8) × line size (512 B) equals 128 KiB, consistent with the L1 instruction cache size reported in Table 3.1 for GV100.
The two-warp thrashing experiment (Figure 3.5, top row) that proves L0 is private to a processing block while L1 is shared across the four processing blocks of an SM.

Code has been implemented that launches 8 warps on one SM with 6 idle, selects two active warps warp A and warp B whose warp indices map (via warp_id % 4) to two different processing blocks, and reports each warp's cycles/instruction independently.

Code has been implemented that first warms a fixed-length measured FFMA sequence (e.g. 1,600 B for the L0-regime experiment, 16,000 B for the L1-regime experiment) in the instruction cache on both warps before any thrashing runs.

Code has been implemented that then executes on warp A a variable-length thrashing FFMA sequence whose length is swept across the L0 or L1 boundary, and re-measures warp A and warp B's inverse throughput on the original measured sequence.

The L0-regime (1,600 B measured sequence) result shows that warp A's inverse throughput rises as the thrashing sequence approaches ~12 KiB while warp B's inverse throughput stays flat, demonstrating L0 is private to a scheduler/processing block.

The L1-regime (16,000 B measured sequence) result shows both warp A and warp B's inverse throughput rise together as the thrashing sequence approaches 128 KiB, demonstrating L1 is shared across processing blocks within an SM.
The two-SM thrashing experiment (Figure 3.5, bottom row) that proves L1 is private to each SM while the unified L2 is shared across all SMs.

Code has been implemented that launches one warp on SM 0 and one warp on SM 1 (pinning via block scheduling or blockIdx→SM checks), each measuring its own cycles/instruction on a fixed-length FFMA sequence.
Code has been implemented that then thrashes only SM 0 with a variable-length FFMA sequence whose length is swept across the L1 boundary (KiB range) and the L2 boundary (MiB range).
In the L1-boundary sweep, SM 0's measured inverse throughput rises as the thrashing sequence approaches 128 KiB while SM 1's stays flat, demonstrating that L1 instruction cache is private to each SM.

In the L2-boundary sweep, both SM 0's and SM 1's measured inverse throughput rise together as the thrashing sequence approaches ~6,144 KiB, demonstrating that the L2 instruction cache is shared across SMs (the unified L2).
Reporting artifacts that consolidate the instruction cache findings into figures and table rows matching the paper.

Code has been implemented that plots the four-panel Figure 3.3-equivalent chart for V100 (L0/L1/L2 plateaus on the KiB range and L2/global transition on the MiB range) with y-axis cycles/instruction and x-axis FFMA sequence size.
Code has been implemented that plots the two-panel Figure 3.4-equivalent chart showing the 16-stage L0 associativity ladder and the 32-stage L1 associativity ladder from the high-resolution sweeps.

Code has been implemented that emits a machine-readable summary (JSON or CSV) with the L0, L1 and L2 instruction cache sizes, line sizes, set counts and associativities so downstream comparison against Table 3.1 rows for GV100 is automatic.

sub_tasks.requirements: The three levels of the constant cache are reproduced with their broadcast latencies (~27, ~89, ~245 cycles), the 2 KiB / >=64 KiB / L2-shared sizes, the L1.5-constant-cache-coincides-with-L1-instruction-cache finding, and the address-divergence serialization latency curves.
Constant memory declaration and benchmark harness supporting warp-uniform and warp-divergent access patterns are implemented.

Code has been implemented that declares a `__constant__` array in device memory of at least 384 KiB (large enough to overflow the L1.5 constant cache) and populates it from the host via `cudaMemcpyToSymbol` so that constant-memory access experiments can be driven from device kernels.

Code has been implemented for a single-warp constant-memory latency kernel that (a) reads a `%clock` cycle counter before and after a dependent chain of constant loads through `ld.const` (or an `LDC` PTX/SASS sequence), (b) uses pointer-chase style dependencies so that memory-level parallelism is disabled, and (c) writes per-thread start/stop timestamps back to global memory for host-side analysis.

Code has been implemented for an address-divergence harness that, for a parameter D in {1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32}, produces per-thread constant addresses such that exactly D distinct addresses are referenced across the 32 threads of a warp (D=1 exercises the broadcast path, D=32 exercises full serialization).
The L1 constant cache geometry (2 KiB size, 64 B line, 8 sets, 4-way associativity, non-LRU) and broadcast latency (~27 cycles) are characterized.

Code has been implemented for a fine-grained constant-memory pointer-chase (or strided-scan) benchmark that sweeps the working-set size across the region 0.25 KiB..4 KiB in steps small enough (<= 128 B) to bracket a 2 KiB capacity boundary and reports per-size average constant-load latency.
The L1 constant cache size on V100 is measured at 2 KiB (the latency step from the L1-hit plateau to the L1.5-hit plateau occurs at a working-set size of 2 KiB, matching Table 3.1).

The measured L1 constant cache broadcast latency on V100 (all 32 threads of a warp accessing the same address, working set fitting in L1) is reported as approximately 27 clock cycles, matching Table 3.1 / Figure 3.7 [Claim 17].
The measured L1 constant cache line size on V100 is reported as 64 B (the cache miss curve advances one miss for every 64 B of stride).
The L1 constant cache is reported as 8 sets and 4-way associative on V100 (matching Table 3.1) as derived from the fine-grained size-sweep experiment.
The L1.5 constant cache geometry (>=64 KiB size, 256 B line) and broadcast latency (~89 cycles) are characterized.

Code has been implemented that sweeps the constant-memory working set through the 4 KiB..128 KiB range to identify the second latency plateau corresponding to L1.5 constant cache hits, using enough stride resolution (<= 1 KiB) to detect the L1.5 capacity boundary.
The L1.5 constant cache size on V100 is measured to be at least 64 KiB (the transition from the L1.5 plateau to the L2 plateau occurs at a working-set size >= 64 KiB, matching Table 3.1).
The measured L1.5 constant cache broadcast latency on V100 (working set exceeds 2 KiB but fits in L1.5) is reported as approximately 89 clock cycles, matching Table 3.1 / Figure 3.7 [Claim 18].
The measured L1.5 constant cache line size on V100 is reported as 256 B, consistent with Table 3.1.
The L2 constant cache latency (~245 cycles) and its identity with the unified L2 cache are characterized.
Code has been implemented that drives the constant-memory working-set size beyond the L1.5 capacity (>= 128 KiB) but within the 6,144 KiB L2 cache to isolate the L2-constant-hit latency plateau.
The measured L2 constant cache broadcast latency on V100 (working set exceeds L1.5 but fits in L2) is reported as approximately 245 clock cycles, matching Table 3.1 / Figure 3.7 [Claim 19].

A cross-check experiment demonstrates that the third level of constant cache is the unified L2 cache (a global-memory-thrash pass that fills the 6,144 KiB L2 evicts constant-memory data and forces DRAM-latency accesses on the next constant load), consistent with the paper's L2-constant/L2-data unification finding.
The finding that the L1.5 constant cache coincides with the L1 instruction cache on Volta is reproduced (Section 3.4, Figure 3.6).

Code has been implemented for a coincidence experiment that interleaves (a) a constant-array scan sized to fit in L1.5 constant cache with (b) an FFMA instruction sequence of parameterized length, executes the constant scan a second time after the FFMA thrash, and reports the L1.5 constant cache miss rate of the second scan as a function of FFMA-sequence size.
The FFMA-sequence size sweep covers 0..384 KiB with enough resolution (<= 8 KiB steps) to observe the full transition of the L1.5 constant cache miss rate from 0% to 100%, matching Figure 3.6.

The measured L1.5 constant cache miss rate starts near 0% for very short FFMA sequences and reaches ~100% by an FFMA-sequence size around the 128 KiB L1 instruction cache capacity, matching the qualitative curve in Figure 3.6 and establishing that L1.5 constant cache and L1 instruction cache coincide.
The per-warp address-divergence serialization latency curves for L1, L1.5 and L2 constant cache (Figure 3.7) are reproduced.

Code has been implemented that reports average per-warp constant-load latency as a function of the number of distinct addresses referenced within the warp (1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32) for each of the three constant cache residency levels (L1, L1.5, L2), separately controlling the working-set size to enforce residency at the desired level.

The measured latency for the D=1 (broadcast) case matches the level-specific base latencies (~27 / ~89 / ~245 cycles for L1 / L1.5 / L2 respectively), verifying that constant-memory accesses to a single address are served in one broadcast.

The measured latency curves are monotonically non-decreasing in the number of distinct addresses D for each of the three cache levels, reflecting the serialization of divergent constant accesses reported in Figure 3.7.

At maximum divergence (D=32 distinct addresses within a warp), the measured latency for the L2-constant residency case reaches approximately 600-700 cycles, matching the top-right end of the L2-const curve in Figure 3.7.
The three latency curves are ordered such that L2-const latency > L1.5-const latency > L1-const latency for every value of D in {1,2,4,8,16,32}, consistent with the ordering shown in Figure 3.7.
Reporting artifacts consolidate the constant-cache findings into the paper-comparable Table 3.1 entries and Figure 3.6/3.7 reproductions.

Code has been implemented that emits a machine-readable results file (e.g. JSON or CSV) containing the measured L1/L1.5/L2 constant-cache broadcast latencies, L1 constant-cache size, line size, sets, associativity, and L1.5 constant-cache size and line size, populating exactly the Table 3.1 constant-cache row for V100.

Code has been implemented that produces plots reproducing Figure 3.6 (L1.5 constant cache miss rate vs. FFMA-sequence size) and Figure 3.7 (constant-load latency vs. distinct addresses per warp, one curve per cache level).

Behavioral checks confirm that the compiled FFMA sweep exercises the intended bank-conflict conditions before any timing claim is made.

The measured outcomes from the FFMA sweep on V100 reproduce the Figure 3.8 / Table 3.1 findings on register banking.

Code has been implemented that provides a global-memory pointer-chase CUDA kernel: each thread dereferences a chain of pointers laid out at a configurable stride across a global array, and each dependent load's latency is what the benchmark records.

The V100 L2 TLB page-entry size measured from the sweep is 32 MiB, matching the 'L2 TLB Page entry 32 MiB' entry in Table 3.1 for V100.

Code has been implemented that emits Figure 3.12-style latency-vs-array-size data (or plot) for V100 with both the 2-MiB-stride and 32-MiB-stride traces overlaid on log-scaled array size in MiB.

Code has been implemented that binary-patches the 21-bit Volta control section of instruction A, exposing the stall-cycles field (0..15), the wait-barrier mask (6 bits), the read-barrier index (3 bits), and the write-barrier index (3 bits), so measurement can sweep these fields without recompiling.

Stall-cycle-decrement methodology for fixed-latency instructions.

Code has been implemented that computes the expected value of A's operation on the host and compares it against the value B observed on the device, classifying each stall setting as correct or incorrect.

Code has been implemented that sweeps A's stall-cycles field over the full 4-bit range (0..15) and records, for each instruction under test, the last (largest-decremented, i.e. smallest) stall value for which B's output is still functionally correct.

Latencies of shared- and global-memory atomicAdd under 1/2/4/8/16/32-thread contention on V100 (Table 4.2) and the four contention scenarios of Figure 4.1 (single-block-contention, single-block-no-contention, multi-block-contention, multi-block-no-contention) are reproduced.
Microbenchmark harness for measuring latency of atomicAdd on shared and global memory under varying contention exists and executes on V100.

Code has been implemented that defines a CUDA kernel issuing atomicAdd() on a 32-bit shared-memory location, with the number of contending threads within a warp parameterizable to 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, and 32.
Code has been implemented that defines a CUDA kernel issuing atomicAdd() on a 32-bit global-memory location, with the number of contending threads parameterizable to 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, and 32.

The latency benchmark follows the paper's (A,B) pair methodology: an atomicAdd instruction A is immediately followed by a load B of known latency accessing the same location, cumulative latency is measured via a CS2R (or %clock) bracket, and A's latency is deduced by subtracting B's known latency.

Code has been implemented that measures the known latency of the follow-up load instruction B once at startup on the target GPU and uses that measured value in the subtraction so the reported atomic latency is in units of clock cycles.

The contention setting is implemented so that exactly N threads within a warp target the same address while the remaining threads are inactive with respect to the atomic (so the reported number corresponds to Table 4.2's 'none/2/4/8/16/32 threads' columns).

Code has been implemented that writes per-configuration measured latencies to a machine-readable file (e.g. results/atomic_latency.csv) with columns for memory space (shared/global), contention count, and cycles.

A behavioral unit test asserts that when the contention count is 1 the measured shared-memory atomic latency is strictly smaller than when the contention count is 32, on any Volta-class GPU used for grading.
V100 shared-memory atomicAdd latency values from Table 4.2 are reproduced within tolerance for every contention level.

Measured V100 shared-memory atomicAdd latency at 2-thread contention matches the paper's Table 4.2 value of 7 clock cycles within tolerance.
Measured V100 shared-memory atomicAdd latency at 4-thread contention matches the paper's Table 4.2 value of 11 clock cycles within tolerance.
Measured V100 shared-memory atomicAdd latency at 8-thread contention matches the paper's Table 4.2 value of 18 clock cycles within tolerance.
Measured V100 shared-memory atomicAdd latency at 16-thread contention matches the paper's Table 4.2 value of 24 clock cycles within tolerance.
Measured V100 shared-memory atomicAdd latency at 32-thread (full-warp) contention matches the paper's Table 4.2 value of 66 clock cycles within tolerance.
V100 global-memory atomicAdd latency values from Table 4.2 are reproduced within tolerance for every contention level.
Measured V100 global-memory atomicAdd latency at 1-thread contention (none) matches the paper's Table 4.2 value of 36 clock cycles within tolerance.
Measured V100 global-memory atomicAdd latency at 2-thread contention matches the paper's Table 4.2 value of 31 clock cycles within tolerance.
Measured V100 global-memory atomicAdd latency at 4-thread contention matches the paper's Table 4.2 value of 32 clock cycles within tolerance.
Measured V100 global-memory atomicAdd latency at 8-thread contention matches the paper's Table 4.2 value of 41 clock cycles within tolerance.
Measured V100 global-memory atomicAdd latency at 16-thread contention matches the paper's Table 4.2 value of 58 clock cycles within tolerance.
Measured V100 global-memory atomicAdd latency at 32-thread (full-warp) contention matches the paper's Table 4.2 value of 76 clock cycles within tolerance.
The four Figure 4.1 atomicAdd throughput contention scenarios are implemented, executed on V100, and produce plots/data matching the paper's qualitative and numerical findings.

Scenario 1 kernel is implemented: one block of 1,024 threads where R threads share one global address and the remaining threads access distinct sequential global addresses grouped 8 to an L2 cache line, with R swept over {1,2,4,...,32}.

Scenario 2 kernel is implemented: one block of 1,024 threads where R threads share one address and the remaining threads access sequential L2 cache lines with each contention group confined to a single L2 line, with R swept over {1,2,4,...,32}.

Scenario 3 kernel is implemented: a variable number of blocks of 1,024 threads each, all threads in all blocks atomicAdd()-ing on the same global address, with the block count swept over {1,2,5,10,20,50,100,300,800}.

Scenario 4 kernel is implemented: a variable number of blocks of 1,024 threads each, where all threads within a block share one address but different blocks target distinct addresses, with the block count swept over the same range as Scenario 3.

Aggregate memory throughput in GB/s is computed for each scenario by dividing total bytes transferred by measured wall time (or from nvprof counters) and saved per-sweep-point to a machine-readable file.
Code has been implemented that generates the four sub-plots of Figure 4.1 (throughput vs. contention count / block count) as image files under results/, one per scenario.

In Scenario 1 (single-block, contention among groups) the peak measured V100 aggregate throughput stays within the paper's <=2 GB/s regime and shows monotonic degradation as the number of contending threads grows from 1 to 32, matching Figure 4.1 top-left.

In Scenario 2 (single-block, no contention among groups) the V100 measured throughput curve stays within the paper's <=2 GB/s regime and does not exceed the P100 curve at any swept contention count, matching Figure 4.1 top-right.
In Scenario 3 (multi-block contention on a single address) the V100 measured aggregate throughput remains below 12 GB/s across the full block-count sweep, matching Figure 4.1 bottom-left.

In Scenario 4 (multi-block, no contention among blocks) the V100 peak measured aggregate throughput reaches the paper's ~200 GB/s regime and strictly exceeds the corresponding P100/P4/M60/K80 curves at the largest block count, matching Figure 4.1 bottom-right.

A summary check in the reproduction confirms the paper's qualitative Figure 4.1 claim: V100 is the top performer only in Scenario 4 (multi-block, no inter-block contention) and is not the top performer in Scenarios 1, 2, or 3.

sub_tasks.requirements: The wmma::mma_sync 16x16x16 half-precision path on Volta is dissected: NVCC lowers it to 4 sets of 4 HMMA.884.F32.F32.STEPk instructions, threads split into 8 groups by group_id = tid/4, each group computes a 4x8 tile of C, and the load/compute/store thread-to-position mappings shown in Figures 4.2, 4.3, 4.4, 4.5, 4.6 and 4.7 are recovered from SASS disassembly and register-level instrumentation.
The build environment and reference wmma kernel needed to expose HMMA lowering are set up on a Volta V100.

Code has been implemented that compiles the tensor-core benchmark with CUDA 9.0 nvcc using `-arch=sm_70` (Volta) and preserves debug symbols/line info sufficient to correlate SASS with source constructs.

Code has been implemented that declares wmma fragments `wmma::fragment<matrix_a, 16, 16, 16, half, col_major>`, `wmma::fragment<matrix_b, 16, 16, 16, half, col_major>` and `wmma::fragment<accumulator, 16, 16, 16, float>` matching the paper's column-major FP16-in / FP32-out example.

Code has been implemented for a single-warp reference kernel that performs one 16x16x16 half-precision matrix multiplication C = A*B by calling `wmma::load_matrix_sync` for A and B, `wmma::mma_sync` once, and `wmma::store_matrix_sync` for C, so that exactly one mma_sync invocation is present for SASS inspection.

Code has been implemented that populates A and B with unique, thread-identifiable half-precision values (e.g. encoding row/column indices) and validates the numerical result of C against a CPU reference so the mapping instrumentation runs on a functionally correct GEMM.
A SASS extraction pipeline turns the compiled reference kernel into a parsed list of HMMA instructions with their operand registers and STEP/set indices.
Code has been implemented that compiles the reference kernel to a cubin for sm_70 and runs `cuobjdump --dump-sass` (or `nvdisasm`) to produce a textual SASS listing of the kernel.

Code has been implemented that parses the SASS listing and extracts, in program order, every HMMA instruction as a record containing the STEP flag (STEP0..STEP3), the destination register, and the two source registers used as A and B fragments.
The lowering of one wmma::mma_sync into HMMA.884.F32.F32 instructions is characterized in structure and count, reproducing Listing 4.1.

The extracted SASS shows that NVCC 9.0 lowers the single `wmma::mma_sync` call into instructions whose opcode/mnemonic is `HMMA.884.F32.F32` (half-precision inputs, FP32 accumulate), i.e. no other HMMA variant is emitted for the mma_sync path.
Measured: the number of HMMA instructions emitted for one wmma::mma_sync 16x16x16 fp16 call equals the paper's value of 16 (4 sets x 4 STEPs), verified by counting HMMA entries in the parsed SASS.
Measured: the 16 HMMA instructions group into exactly 4 sets (as defined by the paper: consecutive STEP0->STEP1->STEP2->STEP3 runs), reproducing the '4 sets' claim from Section 4.3.
Measured: each set contains exactly 4 HMMA instructions and their STEP suffixes appear in the order STEP0, STEP1, STEP2, STEP3, matching Listing 4.1 line-by-line.

The destination C registers of the four HMMA instructions within each set (STEP0, STEP1, STEP2, STEP3) are identical to the destination C registers of the corresponding STEPs in the other three sets (each C-accumulator register is written by all four sets), matching the register-reuse pattern of Listing 4.1.

The A-fragment and B-fragment source registers differ between the four sets while remaining constant within a set (with only .reuse modifiers changing), matching the pattern in Listing 4.1 where set 0 uses (R26,R16), set 1 uses (R20,R18), set 2 uses (R22,R12), and set 3 uses (R2,R14).
The warp is partitioned into thread groups that jointly compute distinct 4x8 tiles of C, reproducing the paper's group_id rule and per-group tile size.
Code has been implemented that, for each thread in the warp, computes and records `group_id = threadIdx.x / 4`, deriving the group membership rule from tid rather than hardcoding it.
Measured: the number of thread groups formed by group_id = tid/4 across the 32-thread warp equals 8, matching the paper's '8 groups' claim.
Measured: every thread group has exactly 4 threads (32 threads / 8 groups), confirmed by counting members of each group_id bucket.

Measured: each thread group is responsible for exactly 4 x 8 = 32 elements of the output matrix C (verified by counting the unique (row,col) C positions written by threads sharing a group_id in the store instrumentation), reproducing the '4x8 tile per group' claim.
The thread-to-position mapping produced by wmma::load_matrix_sync for matrix A is recovered element-by-element and matches Figure 4.2.

Code has been implemented that instruments each thread's `a_frag.x[i]` after `load_matrix_sync` and, using the identifiable A values (row/col encoding), recovers for every (row,col) position of A the set of thread indices that loaded it.
Measured: each thread loads exactly 16 half-precision elements from matrix A into its a_frag, matching the paper's statement that 'every thread loads 16 elements from matrix A'.
Measured: every (row,col) position of matrix A is loaded by exactly two distinct threads of the warp, matching the paper's observation that 'two different threads load from one position in A and B'.

Measured: the full 16x16 table of (position -> pair of thread indices) recovered for matrix A matches Figure 4.2 in the paper exactly (e.g. address 0 -> threads (0,8); address 2 -> (0,8); address 8 -> (16,24); address 128 -> (0,8); address 480 -> (3,11); etc.).
The thread-to-position mapping produced by wmma::load_matrix_sync for matrix B is recovered element-by-element and matches Figure 4.3.
Code has been implemented that instruments each thread's `b_frag.x[i]` after `load_matrix_sync` and recovers, for every (row,col) position of B, the set of thread indices that loaded it.
Measured: each thread loads exactly 16 half-precision elements from matrix B into its b_frag, matching the paper's statement that 'every thread loads 16 elements from B'.

Measured: the full 16x16 table of (position -> pair of thread indices) recovered for matrix B matches Figure 4.3 in the paper exactly (e.g. address 0 -> threads (0,4); address 128 -> (16,20); address 256 -> (8,12); address 384 -> (24,28); etc.).
The intra-group STEP-to-position pattern (Figure 4.4) and the group-to-tile mapping over C (Figure 4.5) are recovered.

The four STEP flags (STEP0..STEP3) of a HMMA set are shown to write four disjoint 2x2 sub-blocks that together tile the group's 4x8 C region, reproducing the STEP0/STEP1/STEP2/STEP3 partition of Figure 4.4.

Measured: the 8 recovered per-group 4x8 tiles collectively tile the full 16x16 output matrix C without overlap, and their positions within C match the group->quadrant mapping in Figure 4.5 (group 0 top-left, group 7 bottom-right, etc.).
The set-to-A/B-slice correspondence of Figure 4.6 is recovered: the four HMMA sets consume distinct K-slices of A and B while writing the same group C tile.

Code has been implemented that, for each of the 4 HMMA sets, associates the set with the K-slice of A and B it multiplies (via the mapping between the set's source A/B registers and the A/B elements loaded into those registers by each thread).

Measured: sets 0, 1, 2 and 3 each consume a distinct, disjoint quarter of the K=16 dimension of A and the corresponding quarter of B (four non-overlapping A column-slabs multiplied by four non-overlapping B row-slabs), and all four sets accumulate into the same 4x8 C tile of the group, reproducing the layout of Figure 4.6.
The thread-to-position mapping written by wmma::store_matrix_sync for matrix C is recovered element-by-element and matches Figure 4.7.

Code has been implemented that, before `store_matrix_sync`, overwrites each thread's `c_frag.x[i]` with an encoding of that thread's index and after storing to memory scans C to derive, for each (row,col) position of C, the thread index that wrote it.

Measured: the full 16x16 table of (position -> thread index) recovered from store_matrix_sync matches Figure 4.7 exactly (e.g. address 0 -> thread 0, address 4 -> thread 1, address 16 -> thread 16, address 512 -> thread 8, address 1020 -> thread 31, etc.), and each thread writes exactly 8 C positions.

Code has been implemented that writes the parsed HMMA sequence to a text artifact grouped by set (set 0..set 3) with STEP0..STEP3 order preserved and destination/source registers listed, producing an output analogous in shape to Listing 4.1.

Code has been implemented that renders the recovered A-load, B-load and C-store thread-to-position mappings as 16x16 tables (or figures) analogous to Figures 4.2, 4.3 and 4.7, and the group-to-C-region and set-to-A/B-slice mappings analogous to Figures 4.5 and 4.6, saved as reproduction artifacts.
