Code has been implemented that computes the V100 theoretical peak TFLOPS values used as the `Theoretical` reference lines in Figure 4.8 (single: 2 * 80 SMs * 64 FP32 cores * 1.380 GHz ≈ 14.13 TFLOPS; double: 2 * 80 * 32 * 1.380 ≈ 7.07 TFLOPS; half via tensor cores: 2 * 80 * 8 * 128 * 1.380 ≈ 125 TFLOPS).
Single-precision cuBLAS SGEMM benchmarking on V100@1,380 MHz reproduces the Figure 4.8 single-precision curve and its near-peak claim.

Code has been implemented that invokes `cublasSgemm` on FP32 input matrices of size N x N (N in {2048,4096,6144,8192}), performs at least one warm-up call, and times the operation with CUDA events or `cudaDeviceSynchronize()` around a repeated inner loop to derive an accurate TFLOPS number.

Code has been implemented that converts SGEMM elapsed time into TFLOPS via 2*N^3 / (time_seconds * 1e12) for each matrix size and writes a machine-readable table (e.g. CSV/JSON) containing size, elapsed time, and measured TFLOPS.

The measured cuBLAS SGEMM throughput on the V100 at 1,380 MHz reaches near-peak single-precision performance (approaching ~14 TFLOPS theoretical) at the larger matrix sizes, matching the `Measured` curve in the Single Precision subplot of Figure 4.8.
Double-precision cuBLAS DGEMM benchmarking on V100@1,380 MHz reproduces the Figure 4.8 double-precision curve and its near-peak claim.

Code has been implemented that invokes `cublasDgemm` on FP64 input matrices of size N x N (N in {2048,4096,6144,8192}), warms up the call, and times it with CUDA events / `cudaDeviceSynchronize()` to compute TFLOPS.

The measured cuBLAS DGEMM throughput on the V100 at 1,380 MHz reaches near-peak double-precision performance (approaching ~7 TFLOPS theoretical) at the larger matrix sizes, matching the `Measured` curve in the Double Precision subplot of Figure 4.8.

Half-precision cuBLAS HGEMM benchmarking on the V100 tensor cores at 1,380 MHz reproduces the Figure 4.8 half-precision curves (both 16-bit and 32-bit accumulator variants) and the 90.2%-of-theoretical claim.

Code has been implemented that dispatches half-precision GEMM through cuBLAS with `cublasSetMathMode(..., CUBLAS_TENSOR_OP_MATH)` (or the equivalent `CUBLAS_GEMM_DFALT_TENSOR_OP` algo passed to `cublasGemmEx`) so that HMMA tensor core instructions are used rather than falling back to CUDA cores.

Code has been implemented that runs two half-precision cuBLAS GEMM variants — one accumulating in FP16 (labeled `16bit-result` in Figure 4.8) and one accumulating in FP32 (labeled `32bit-result`) — over the matrix sweep 2048/4096/6144/8192, matching the two `Measured` curves in the Half Precision subplot.

Code has been implemented that computes half-precision TFLOPS as 2*N^3/(time_seconds*1e12) per matrix size and per accumulator width, and records elapsed time / TFLOPS / theoretical-throughput ratio into a machine-readable output.

The peak measured half-precision HGEMM throughput on V100 tensor cores at 1,380 MHz reaches 90.2% (within tolerance) of the theoretical tensor-core throughput reported in Section 4.4 / Figure 4.8, i.e. approximately 113 TFLOPS versus the ~125 TFLOPS peak.

The measured HGEMM TFLOPS values monotonically increase with matrix size and are highest at N=8192 for both 16-bit and 32-bit result accumulator variants, matching the trend of the Half Precision subplot of Figure 4.8.
Figure 4.8 is regenerated from the collected SGEMM/DGEMM/HGEMM measurements, with the three subplots (single, double, half) showing measured vs. theoretical TFLOPS across the four matrix sizes.

Code has been implemented that consumes the benchmark output CSV/JSON and emits a Figure 4.8 replica image with three vertically stacked panels (Half Precision, Single Precision, Double Precision), each plotting `Measured` and `Theoretical` curves versus matrix size, with matching axis units (TFLOPS vs. Matrix Size).

The regenerated Figure 4.8 shows, for each of the four matrix sizes, the measured single- and double-precision TFLOPS approaching their respective theoretical curves at N >= 4096, and the half-precision measured curves reaching ~90% of the theoretical tensor-core curve at N=8192.

The V100 NVLink 2.0 findings from Chapter 5 are reproduced: up to 6 sub-links per GPU at 25 GB/s per sub-link per direction (up to 300 GB/s aggregate), peer-to-peer latencies and bandwidths measured on V100 NVLink and compared against V100 PCIe and P100 NVLink 1.0 (Table 5.1), plus arithmetic/memory throughput and latency measurements at the 1,530 MHz SXM2 clock (Sections 5.2 and 5.3).

The multi-GPU benchmark environment required to reproduce Chapter 5 is set up: three configurations (V100 SXM2/NVLink 2.0, V100 PCIe Gen 3, P100 SXM2/NVLink 1.0) can be selected, clocks are pinned to their reported peak, and the NVLink topology is queried.

Code has been implemented that detects a V100 SXM2 board with NVLink 2.0 (via `cudaDeviceGetAttribute` compute capability 7.0 and presence of NVLink links reported by NVML) and refuses to run the NVLink section on a machine where no NVLink-capable V100 is present.

Code has been implemented that identifies the two baseline reference configurations (V100 PCIe and P100 NVLink) either from live devices or from cached numeric fixtures loaded from a documented location, so that all three Table 5.1 rows can be assembled.

Code has been implemented that pins each GPU to its paper-stated peak graphics clock (V100 NVLink at 1,530 MHz, V100 PCIe at 1,380 MHz, P100 PCIe at 1,328 MHz) via `nvidia-smi -ac`/`--lock-gpu-clocks` before running any Chapter 5 benchmark and verifies the applied clock by reading it back.

Code has been implemented that parses `nvidia-smi topo -m` (or the equivalent NVML `nvmlDeviceGetNvLinkCapability`) to enumerate, for every GPU pair, the number of NVLink sub-links and the connection type (NVLink vs PCIe), producing a topology table used to drive the P2P benchmarks.
Peer-to-peer bandwidth measurements from Section 5.1 are reproduced across the V100 NVLink, V100 PCIe and P100 NVLink configurations, populating the bandwidth columns of Table 5.1.

Code has been implemented that measures peer-to-peer bandwidth via a CUDA benchmark using `cudaMemcpyPeerAsync` on a warmed-up, page-locked buffer sized to saturate NVLink (>=256 MiB), sweeping unidirectional and bidirectional transfers and reporting the sustained GB/s for each ordered device pair.

The P2P bandwidth benchmark, when run on a synthetic loopback (same device as source and destination) or a scripted mock topology, produces a symmetric bandwidth matrix and correctly separates unidirectional from bidirectional totals so that a bidirectional total equals the sum of the two unidirectional halves (within 5%).
The measured number of NVLink 2.0 sub-links available to a V100 SXM2 GPU is up to 6 (as reported for NVLink-connected V100 pairs), matching the Section 5.1 claim.
The measured per-sub-link, per-direction unidirectional bandwidth of NVLink 2.0 on V100 approaches the theoretical 25 GB/s, matching the value reported at the start of Section 5.1.
The aggregate bidirectional interconnect bandwidth measured to a V100 SXM2 GPU across all six NVLink 2.0 sub-links reaches up to 300 GB/s, matching the Section 5.1 headline number.

The measured V100 NVLink 2.0 peer-to-peer bandwidth for a single-link pair is substantially higher than the V100 PCIe Gen 3 P2P bandwidth measured on the same benchmark, reproducing the Table 5.1 qualitative ordering (NVLink 2.0 >> PCIe Gen 3).
The measured V100 NVLink 2.0 per-sub-link bandwidth exceeds the P100 NVLink 1.0 per-sub-link bandwidth in the same benchmark, matching the NVLink-generation improvement documented in Table 5.1.
Peer-to-peer and host-to-device latency measurements from Section 5.1 are reproduced and populate the latency columns of Table 5.1.

Code has been implemented that measures peer-to-peer transfer latency by timing a very small (single cache-line) `cudaMemcpyPeerAsync` on a warmed link with CUDA events, averaged over many repetitions to yield a stable microsecond-scale figure per ordered device pair.

Code has been implemented that measures host-to-device and device-to-host transfer bandwidth and latency over pinned host memory across each of the three configurations (V100 NVLink, V100 PCIe, P100 NVLink) so that Table 5.1's host communication columns can be filled.

The measured single-hop P2P latency on V100 NVLink 2.0 is reported alongside V100 PCIe and P100 NVLink 1.0 values, and the three-way ordering matches the Table 5.1 ordering (NVLink 2.0 latency is on the order of the P100 NVLink 1.0 latency and lower than the V100 PCIe P2P latency).

Arithmetic throughput and memory bandwidth measurements on the NVLink V100 (Section 5.2) are reproduced at the 1,530 MHz peak clock and compared against the PCIe V100 (1,380 MHz) numbers reported earlier in the paper.

Code has been implemented that re-runs the cuBLAS SGEMM/DGEMM/HGEMM benchmarks from Section 4.4 on the V100 NVLink board at 1,530 MHz, producing TFLOPS results for a matrix-size sweep matching the paper's Figure 4.8 axes (2048, 4096, 6144, 8192).

The measured SGEMM, DGEMM and HGEMM peak throughput on the V100 NVLink at 1,530 MHz scales relative to the 1,380 MHz PCIe measurements approximately in proportion to the clock ratio (1530/1380 ~= 1.109), within a documented tolerance.

The HBM2 global memory bandwidth benchmark (a stream-style copy of one global array to another) is executed on the V100 NVLink board and its measured GB/s is reported alongside the V100 PCIe measurement (~750 GiB/s at 83.3% of the 900 GiB/s theoretical).
Latency measurements on the NVLink V100 (Section 5.3) are reproduced and compared against the PCIe V100 numbers to demonstrate that the SXM2 form factor does not change on-chip latency behavior.

Code has been implemented that re-runs the native instruction dependent-issue latency benchmark from Section 4.1 on the V100 NVLink board, emitting per-instruction latencies for the same instruction set (IADD3, FFMA, IMAD, DFMA, MUFU, etc.) as reported for the PCIe V100.

The dependent-issue latencies measured on V100 NVLink match those measured on V100 PCIe within 1 cycle for every instruction in Table 4.1, confirming Section 5.3's claim that form factor does not perturb instruction latency.

The L1 data cache hit latency (28 cycles) and L2 cache hit latency (~193 cycles) measured on V100 NVLink match, within tolerance, the PCIe V100 numbers reported in Table 3.1, confirming that the memory hierarchy latencies from Chapter 3 also hold on the SXM2 board.
The measured Chapter 5 numbers are collected into a single reproducible artifact that mirrors the layout and rows of Table 5.1 and can be diffed against the paper's published table.

Code has been implemented that assembles the per-pair P2P bandwidth, P2P latency and host-communication numbers into a CSV/JSON table with one row per (source-device, dest-device) pair and columns matching Table 5.1's headers.

The reproduced Table 5.1 artifact contains all three interconnect configurations reported in the paper: V100 NVLink (NVLink 2.0), V100 PCIe (PCIe Gen 3), and P100 NVLink (NVLink 1.0); missing hardware rows are permitted but must be marked as such rather than silently omitted or fabricated.

A single `reproduce_chapter5.sh` (or equivalent) driver script exists that runs the P2P bandwidth, P2P latency, host-communication, arithmetic throughput and instruction-latency benchmarks end-to-end and writes the resulting Table 5.1 artifact plus the three headline NVLink numbers (6 sub-links, 25 GB/s per sub-link, 300 GB/s aggregate) to `results/`.
